pre_event_materials: Generic React starter kit written by the team before the event and committed as the repository's first commit, 'Starter kit baseline'. Vite + React 19 + Tailwind 4 shell (index.html, src/main.jsx, src/App.jsx, src/app.css), a localStorage/Supabase storage adapter (src/lib/db.js), a library of thirteen generic self-contained capability modules with their own tests (src/recipes/), five accessible colour palettes (src/themes/), and helper scripts (scripts/preflight.sh, scripts/smoke-live.sh, scripts/compress-video.sh). It contains no solution to P10 or to any other released problem; it was written before the problems were known. Declared in full in EVENT.md.
Documentation templates from the same starter kit: README-TEMPLATE.md, SUBMISSION-TEMPLATE.md, LICENSES.md, BOARD.md, DEPLOY.md, CLAUDE.md.

sample_data.method: seeded on start; all 25 published cases in a Household selector; CSV or JSON paste and upload; a set-up form for a household without a file
sample_data.reset_instructions: The published fixture case PUB-01 is bundled and loads for any first-time visitor. A household the user loads or sets up is remembered in that browser only; the header's 'Back to the sample' button (and clearing site data) returns to PUB-01. To load a different case, pick one of the 25 in the Household selector, or paste/upload CSV or JSON on the household step — the accepted formats are stated beside the control, and malformed input is refused naming the field or row at fault.

problem_solving_method: The tariff is the entire problem, so it is built as a pure module with a node --test suite written before any user interface, and the interface reads from it. All money is handled in integer paisa and converted to taka only at the render edge, because the balance compounds across 181 days and floating point drift would put every downstream answer slightly wrong. The organizers' published fixture shape was adopted directly as the application's data model rather than designing a schema and mapping onto it, so an unpublished case in the same shape loads without a translation layer. Each of the four required items is owned by exactly one unit on its own branch and its own files.

R1.evidence: Step "The household" (R1 in the sidebar) opens on fixture case PUB-01 from the organizers' published P10 sample data - 181 consecutive daily readings from 2026-01-01 to 2026-06-30 with 18 recharges - and the header names the lightest month (2026-01, 129 units), the heaviest (2026-05, 673 units) and the month whose largest recharge falls in its last seven days (2026-05, BDT 4,300.00 on 26 May). All three labels are computed from whatever case is loaded, not hard-coded. Another case can be pasted or uploaded, including the whole 25-case pack file.

R2.evidence: Step "Where the money went" (R2). The engine rebuilds the balance day by day in integer paisa: each day's units are charged at the slab the calendar month's running total has reached, the counter resets on the 1st and is never reset by a recharge, the demand charge and meter rent are taken once per month on that month's first recharge, and VAT is 5 percent of the energy amount only. On PUB-01 this gives energy BDT 13,844.79, VAT BDT 692.24, fixed charges BDT 492.00 over six months and a closing balance of BDT 2,080.97 on 30 June. The balance is drawn as a line over the whole period with a marker at every recharge and month boundaries visible; selecting a day shows its units, the slab rate charged and the month running total. Covered by 37 tests over every slab boundary, the month rollover and the once-per-month fixed charges.

R3.evidence: Step "When to recharge" (R3), with the same figures on the overview. From the closing balance and the household's usual daily use the app projects forward day by day, still respecting the calendar-month slab reset, and names the date the balance runs out - 20 July 2026 on PUB-01 at 19 units a day, with the assumption stated on screen. A target-date input, defaulting to the case's own target date, shows what must be recharged today: on PUB-01 to last to 13 August 2026 the days cost BDT 5,600.70 - energy 3,870.68, the part caused by being in a higher slab 1,307.13, fixed charges 164.00 and VAT 258.89 - and the deposit needed is BDT 3,519.73 after the 2,080.97 already on the meter. The four parts reconcile to the cost on screen, and the baseline used for the higher-slab part is stated because the problem does not define one.

R4.evidence: Step "Which habit is cheaper" (R4). Both habits run over the case's three comparison months on identical daily consumption and the same calendar-month slab counter, per R-16, starting from the case's opening balance. Cost is what the meter consumes - energy, VAT and the applicable monthly fixed charges - per R-33, not the amount deposited. Each habit shows its energy, VAT, fixed charges, total and the recharge dates it produced, the cheaper habit is named with the difference, and a sentence states that any difference comes only from how many monthly first-recharge fixed charges occurred. Verified against an independently computed reference over all 25 published cases: energy and VAT are identical between the habits in every case, 22 cases come out equal and three (PUB-02, PUB-06, PUB-24) differ by exactly BDT 82.00, the one month of fixed charges the low-balance habit avoids.

major_design_decisions: The organizers' published fixture shape is the application's data model, rather than a schema of our own with a mapping layer, so that an unpublished case in the same shape loads unchanged.

All money is computed in integer paisa and formatted as taka only at the render edge. The balance compounds over 181 days of daily charges, and floating point drift there would put the run-out date and the habit comparison quietly wrong.
The slab counter is keyed to the calendar month and is never reset by a recharge, which is the single behaviour the problem statement warns produces the wrong number everywhere if inverted.

The demand charge and meter rent are applied once per calendar month on that month's first recharge, so a month with no recharge incurs neither — this is the only mechanism by which the two recharge habits can differ in cost.

For the required recharge breakdown, energy is every projected unit priced at the lowest slab and the higher-slab part is the real slab-aware cost minus that base, so the four parts reconcile exactly to the total. The problem does not define this baseline, so ours is stated on screen.
known_limitations: A meter the user sets up is saved in that browser only; the published sample households and pasted or uploaded cases are not saved, so a first-time visitor always opens on the seeded household. There are no accounts and no server, and the household can be downloaded as JSON.

The organizers' format_note for P10 is truncated mid-sentence where it explains a comparison source other than "readings", so that path is an assumption: a non-"readings" source uses comparison.daily_units as a flat figure for every day of the three months. All 25 published cases use "readings", where the case's own daily readings are used.

The problem does not define a baseline for "the part caused by being in a higher slab". Ours is every projected unit priced at the lowest slab rate, with the higher-slab part being the real slab-aware cost minus that base, so the four parts reconcile exactly. The definition is stated on screen.
The run-out projection assumes the household keeps consuming its stated usual daily units every day, with no seasonal variation and no further recharge.

VAT is rounded once over the energy amount for the period rather than per day and summed, so a figure recomputed with per-day rounding can differ by a few paisa over six months (0.26 taka at most across the published cases). The rows still sum exactly to the totals shown.
Item 3 answers for the days from the first unconsumed day onward; today itself is already charged in the day-by-day rebuild.

ai_tools_used.used_for: Reading and reconciling the organizer documents, authoring the build specification in SPEC.md, and implementing units against it.
ai_tools_used.how_output_was_verified: The tariff rules are covered by a node --test suite exercising every slab boundary, the calendar-month reset, and the once-per-month fixed charges. The habit comparison is additionally checked against an independently computed reference table of the expected answer for all 25 published cases, recorded at the end of SPEC.md. Every required item was checked by a team member on the deployed URL, not locally, before being recorded as done.
